						<div class="post">
				<p class="post-date">Thu 9 Nov 2006</p>
<div class="post-info"><h2 class="post-title"><a href="http://comonad.com/reader/2006/generalizing-dot/" rel="bookmark" title="Permanent Link: Generalizing (.)">Generalizing (.)</a></h2>
Posted by Edward Kmett under <a href="http://comonad.com/reader/category/haskell/" title="View all posts in Haskell" rel="category tag">Haskell</a> ,  <a href="http://comonad.com/reader/category/monads/" title="View all posts in Monads" rel="category tag">Monads</a> <br/><a href="http://comonad.com/reader/2006/generalizing-dot/#comments" title="Comment on Generalizing (.)">[7] Comments</a>&nbsp;</div>
<div class="post-content">
	<p>If we take a look at the Haskell (.) operator:</p>
<p><code type="haskell"><br />
(.) :: (a -> b) -> (e -> a) -> e -> b<br />
</code></p>
<p>and take a moment to reflect on the type of fmap</p>
<p><code type="haskell"><br />
fmap :: Functor f => (a -> b) -> f a -> f b<br />
</code></p>
<p>and the unnamed Reader monad from <a href="http://haskell.org/ghc/docs/latest/html/libraries/mtl/Control-Monad-Reader.html">Control.Monad.Reader</a></p>
<p><code type="haskell"><br />
instance Functor ((->) r)<br />
</code></p>
<p>we see that fmap applied to the Reader functor rederives (.).</p>
<p><span id="more-35"></span></p>
<p><code type="haskell"><br />
fmap_reader :: (a -> b) -> (e -> a) -> e -> b<br />
</code></p>
<p>So if we were willing to forgo ease of learning, and to bake in the Reader monad as a primitive, we could quite concisely redefine (.) to give it a more general signature:</p>
<p><code type="haskell"><br />
module Dot where<br />
import Control.Monad.Reader<br />
import Prelude hiding ((.))<br />
infixr 0 .<br />
(.) :: Functor f => (a -> b) -> f a -> f b<br />
(.) = fmap<br />
</code></p>
<p>In this context, existing code continues to type check. For instance,</p>
<p><code type="haskell"><br />
((+2) . (*3)) 5 ==> 17<br />
</code></p>
<p>And the . above doubles as filling the role of the * map operator mentioned in Richard Bird's 1990 Calculus of Functions paper generalized to any Functor.</p>
<p><code type="haskell"><br />
((+2) . (*3)) . [1..10] ==> [5,8,..32]<br />
((+2) . (*3)) . Just 5 ==> Just 17<br />
((+2) . (*3)) . Nothing ==> Nothing<br />
</code></p>
<p>I was able to test this with the just about every example golfed back and forth on the <a href="irc://irc.freenode.net/%23haskell">#haskell</a> channel in the last 6 months.</p>
<p>I'm not advocating this as a practice for Haskell as it is somewhat terrifying to think of how to teach to new programmers, but I found the exercise to be enlightening.</p>
	<div class="post-info">
			</div>
	<div class="post-footer">&nbsp;</div>
</div>

			<p>I think you need doubled parens when hiding (.) in the import (the outer ones are part of the hiding syntax, the inner ones refer to the infix composition symbol in parens for lexical reasons). Both hugs and ghci seem to like it this way. (Perhaps something in your text chain snarfed the &#8220;redundant&#8221; parens?)</p>
		</li>
